query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a post-synthesis thermal treatment—comprising high‐temperature solutionizing, rapid quenching, and subsequent low-temperature annealing—to as‐cast single‐phase BCC NbMoTaW will induce a controlled dual‐phase microstructure (a continuous, disordered BCC matrix with finely dispersed coherent B2 nano-precipitates) that simultaneously enhances room-temperature ductility and mitigates irradiation-induced defects while retaining high-temperature strength up to 1600 °C.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, as-cast single-phase BCC NbMoTaW with high-temperature strength but poor room-temperature ductility and unverified experimental irradiation tolerance.
generation.intervention: A designed thermal/thermomechanical treatment sequence: first a high-temperature solutionizing step to homogenize the alloy, followed by a rapid quench to freeze in a metastable state, and then a low-temperature anneal to promote the formation of finely dispersed, coherent B2-type nano-precipitates within a disordered BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Mechanical testing performed at room temperature (for ductility) and up to 1600 °C (for high-temperature strength), combined with controlled helium irradiation experiments under conditions representative of reactor environments.
generation.structural_mediator: A nanoscale dual-phase architecture consisting of a ductile, disordered BCC matrix interspersed with coherent nano-precipitates (B2-type regions) that serve as internal defect sinks.
generation.mechanism: The thermal treatment disrupts long-range order and precipitates nanometer-scale particles that enhance dislocation mobility (improving ductility) and act as sinks for irradiation-induced defects (minimizing the formation of amorphous zones, blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation) without compromising the integrity of the primary BCC phase.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated NbMoTaW, the post-treated alloy is expected to exhibit significantly improved room-temperature tensile ductility and reduced irradiation-induced damage (e.g., smaller or fewer helium bubbles and less blistering) while retaining comparable high yield strength and microstructural stability at temperatures up to 1600 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated, as-cast NbMoTaW, which displays high temperature strength but suffers from poor room-temperature ductility and uncertain irradiation tolerance.
generation.boundary: Effective under standard laboratory mechanical testing conditions at room temperature and elevated temperatures up to 1600 °C; irradiation tests should mimic helium implantation or neutron irradiation conditions typical of fusion reactor environments.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of improvements in ductility and irradiation tolerance remains to be determined; additionally, it is uncertain whether the induced nano-precipitate structure will remain stable under prolonged irradiation or thermal cycling.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of NbMoTaW samples: one set as-cast (control) and one subjected to the proposed high-temperature solutionizing, rapid quench, and low-temperature annealing treatment. Perform comprehensive tensile testing at room temperature and high-temperature compressive or tensile tests at up to 1600 °C. Additionally, expose both sets to controlled helium ion irradiation under identical fluence and energy conditions. Compare compared microstructural evolution using transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to assess nano-precipitate formation, defect density, and irradiation-induced features such as bubble formation or amorphization.
measurements: Room-temperature tensile ductility (elongation to failure, tensile strength)
Irradiation-induced defect metrics (size and density of helium bubbles, blistering incidence) via TEM and/or scanning electron microscopy (SEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the post-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in room-temperature ductility and a reduction in irradiation-induced damage (with maintained high-temperature mechanical performance) relative to the untreated control, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Various industrial and advanced functional applications require materials with high strength and ductility. Unfortunately, conventional processing strategies usually attain high material strength at the expense of deteriorated ductility [1] – [3] , whilst developing structures with substantial improvement of both strength and ductility is highly challenging. Recent successes in synthesizing superhard materials [4] – [6] have made the high-pressure and high-temperature (HPHT) treatment [7] , [8] promising to achieve extreme properties in materials. The combination of pressure and temperature offers the great prospect for altering the microstructure of structural materials that would permit overcoming the strength-ductility trade-off. Given the vast space of control parameters involved in the HPHT treatment and the often complex microstructural evolution under extreme pressures and temperatures [9] , [10] , it remains difficult to predict and interpret the mechanical behaviors of HPHT-treated structural materials, especially the abnormal kinetics and thermodynamics of non-equilibrium interfaces induced by the HPHT treatment [11] , [12] .

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure [1] – [3] . These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C [4] , [5] . Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm 3 ) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added [6] – [13] . Key components in magnetic fusion reactors, such as the divertor or the plasma-facing materials (PFMs), are required to have stringent properties including low activation, high melting point, good thermomechanical properties, low sputter erosion, and low tritium retention/codeposition. They must operate at high temperature (≥1000 K) for long durations (>10 7 s), without failure or extensive erosion while exposed to large plasma heat and an intense mixture of ionized and energetic neutral species of hydrogen isotopes (D and T), He ash (fluxes, >10 24 m −2 s −1 ), and neutrons ( [1] ). Tungsten (W) is the leading PFM candidate because of its high melting temperature, low erosion rates, and small tritium retention. These advantages are unfortunately coupled with very low fracture toughness characterized by brittle transgranular and intergranular failure regimes, which severely restrict the useful operating temperature window and also create a range of fabrication difficulties. Furthermore, blistering at moderate temperature (<800 K) by D and He ( [2] , [3] ) and the formation of pits, holes, and bubbles by He at higher temperature (>1600 K) ( [4] ) have all been observed. decision.trend: Early work on refractory high‐entropy alloys highlighted the trade‐off between high‐temperature strength and room‐temperature brittleness. Studies such as PMC5995863 demonstrated that tuning the internal ordering via thermal and thermomechanical treatments (e.g., solutionizing, quenching, and annealing) can dramatically improve room‐temperature ductility by partially disordering an otherwise brittle ordered matrix while retaining high yield strength. In parallel, investigations like PMC6397024 explored radiation response in tungsten-based refractory alloys, revealing that nanoscale precipitation and microstructural heterogeneity can suppress the formation of deleterious defects (dislocation loops, cavities, blistering) under irradiation. These efforts followed the progression from as‐cast, single‐phase alloys with excellent high-temperature performance but poor ductility and unconfirmed irradiation tolerance to microstructure‐engineered alloys that attempt to provide ductile matrices and defect sinks. However, these approaches have not yet been directly applied to equal‐atomic BCC NbMoTaW.
decision.unsolved: The outstanding challenge is to modify NbMoTaW in a way that markedly improves room‐temperature ductility and experimental irradiation tolerance—by providing effective defect sinks—while fully maintaining the single-phase, BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance up to 1600 °C. Neither simple alloying (which risks destabilizing the BCC phase) nor drastic processing changes that induce other phases are acceptable, leaving a gap in a controlled microstructure tailoring approach that simultaneously addresses both mechanical and irradiation-induced failure modes.
decision.lever: Design and optimize a post-synthesis thermal treatment sequence (high-temperature solutionizing followed by rapid quench and a low-temperature anneal) to induce a controlled nanoscale dual-phase architecture (a continuous, disordered BCC matrix with finely dispersed, coherent nano-precipitates, e.g. of ordered B2-type regions).
decision.why: This approach follows the trend observed in earlier refractory HEA studies: tailoring the microstructure via controlled heat treatments can convert a brittle ordered state into one with improved ductility while also introducing nanoscale precipitates that act as defect sinks to enhance irradiation tolerance. It builds directly on the successes observed in PMC5995863 for improving room-temperature ductility and leverages defect recombination mechanisms noted in irradiation studies (PMC6397024) without compromising the BCC phase stability and high-temperature strength of NbMoTaW.
